title: Fairweather's Companion to the Octave, by Road, River and Sky
author: Jasper Fairweather, Gentleman, of No Fixed Abode
origin: Port Cantabile, printed on Broadsheet Row
summary: A cheerful and not entirely trustworthy guide to every realm of the continent, revised by its author after the Cascade with as little alarm as possible.
text: TO THE READER OF THIS FOURTH EDITION

The first three editions of this Companion were received with a warmth I have never been able to account for. Since the third edition certain alterations have occurred in the world. I have noted them wherever a reader wrote to complain, and I have left the rest as it was, on the principle that a guide which changes every time the world does will never be finished, and must be paid for.
THE RESONANT REACH

The orchard country of the west, and the kindest country I know. The birdsong is in tune, which the visitor will find charming for very nearly a week. The oaks ring like bronze when the wind moves them, and a man felling one sounds like a bell-founder dropping his stock. Greet a Reach man with "Does it ring?" and he will answer "True enough", and you will have made a friend for the length of a cider.

At Oakhaven, take your cider at the Boar and Dulcimer, whose hearth has not gone out in ninety years because letting it go out would be an admission. Order the moot-curd, a sharp white cheese aged beside a humming stone, which tastes faintly of thunder. At Wethercombe on the sheep-walk the drovers' house will give you the best mutton of your life and the worst bed. At Stillwater Landing, pay the lock dues in advance. They are not refunded. Do not ask about the board.
The Reach murmurs since the Cascade. So should you. A gentleman who has been told to lower his voice in four realms says this with authority.
THE DAWNING HEIGHTS

Sol-Luminary, the city that hangs from the mountain on chains, was for three editions my chief recommendation, and the reader will find my old chapter on its tiers, its rose-gardens and the rising chord of its dawn reprinted unchanged at the back, because I could not bear to cut it.

At present the upper tiers are closed to visitors on account of the light, which since the year before last has been taking more than it gives. The Umbral Tiers on the city's undersides are open, and very welcoming, in a whisper. Windows there are painted black. Do not bring a mirror; it is not merely that they will fine you. Children are taught to walk in the shade of the person ahead, and I recommend the custom to adults, especially if you can find a tall friend. I travelled the whole of the lower city in the shade of a chain-yard foreman named, he said, nothing that concerned me.
CINDERHOLD

Basalt and soot, eleven tiers into a burning caldera, and the Great Beat over all of it like the heart of a sleeping giant. The people speak between the hammer-falls and greet you with "Still standing." The visitor will find himself pausing in his speech in time with the Beat for the rest of his life, which my publisher says explains a great deal about my prose. Do not drink the slag-wine. I say this as a man who drank it.
THE IRON PEAKS

At Fortis you will be asked "You're heavy?" The correct answer is "Heavy enough." Do not answer, as I did, "Very, thank you, it is the mutton." Weight wanders in the mountains since the bleeding began, and a shield may weigh eighty pounds on a wet morning and nothing at noon. Do not offer your hand to a stranger. I have never learned why, and when I asked, nobody would put a weight on the answer.
THE SHIFTING DUNES

Sandglass Bazaar sits under a dome of acoustic glass two miles across, which breaks the singing of the sand into a soft white hiss, and throws rainbows on your coffee. The greeting is "For how long?" and it is a real question; have an answer. Everything has a term in the Dunes. Marriage has a term. Grief has a term. The visitor who grieves past his term is thought indecent.

I had meant to describe the orchard-city of Veridia, on the shore of the Glass Sea, and had written half a page on its apricots, when I learned that since the Cascade it has been living the same twenty-four seconds over and over. I leave the half page in. The apricots were, I am assured, excellent, and are.
THE TEMPEST ARCHIPELAGO

Port Cantabile climbs its cliff from the Long Mole by the Salt Stair, six wet flights with shops on the landings, and every shroud in the harbour carries a chime. Greet a sailor with "What's she singing?" and he will tell you the key of the tide, and from it the hour, and from that whether you may have a drink yet. Do not run on an open deck. Do not buy a bottle with a name on the label as a souvenir, however good the price. The Free Captains read their Articles aloud in the voice of a man reading a tide-table, and enforce them in the same voice from the derrick on the Mole-head, so mind them.
THE SPECTRAL WOODS

Whisper-Grove is the most courteous city in the world. They will call you "little traveller" however large you are, and "my dear one" by the second evening, and they will mean it. Go down to the Weeping Plaza on a festival night, when the lamps are floated on the long basin under the colonnade. Go out along the Cloister road and listen at the gate of the charitable choir, where the children sing very low and very clear. I have heard nothing lovelier in my travels, and I have been about.
THE ORGANUM

There is nothing to see. That is rather the point of it. Registry Square is grey stone and brass plates and pigeons, and there is a coffee stall there that has stood above half a century, whose keeper has served the clerks every morning and has never once asked what they do. I recommend the coffee and his example.
THE CONTINENTAL RIFT

I have not been to Null-Watch, and the reader is advised to go to considerable lengths not to be sent. Since last year the wall has had something to watch. Those who have come back say the garrison never stops talking, which I had thought would suit me, until a man who had been there looked at me for some time in a tavern and said that it would not.
BY SKY

The skyship is the gentleman's road, if the gentleman has money and no particular wish to arrive. Every vessel aloft rides on a Fortis-cut core that takes the weight off her, and hangs from a tank or two of drift-glass, which wants above all things to be somewhere else. Choose a captain who laughs a good deal. You will not regret it until the moment you understand why he does.
A WORD ON COMING HOME

I am asked, by those who have read the previous editions with care, whether I have in fact been to all of these places. I have been to most of them once, and to some of them in the company of men who had been, which is nearly the same thing; and to the Reach I have been more times than I can count, because I was born there, and it is where I go when the roads are unkind.

So here is the whole of my wisdom, and it is cheaper than the book. The best inn on the continent is the one whose landlord remembers your name. Go out while there is still the whole of it to see. Then come home, and lower your voice, and tell them what you saw.
The world is wide, and since the Cascade a quarter-tone flat, and I recommend it without reserve.
notes: Canon: Series Bible Part VI (realms; Sol-Luminary hung on chains, the Bleach, Umbral Tiers, black-painted windows, mirrors illegal, children walk in the shade; Cinderhold and the Great Beat; Fortis gravity-tides and the eighty-pound shield; Sandglass dome, Veridia's twenty-four-second loop; Port Cantabile on singing coral with carillon rigging) and Part IV (the World Went Flat, a quarter-tone wrong). Vol II Realms I-VIII dialect greetings ("Does it ring?" / "True enough"; "Still standing"; "You're heavy?" / "Heavy enough"; "For how long?"; "What's she singing?") and the Boar and Dulcimer's ninety-year hearth, moot-curd (Vol I III.1). Vol V §1 (do not offer your hand). Vol IV Book Three (the Salt Stair's six flights, Long Mole, derrick and the Articles read like tide-tables) and Book Two (Registry Square's sixty-year coffee stall; written in 414 so "above half a century"). Manuscript Ch14 (the Weeping Plaza's colonnade and festival lamps on the basin before 416), Requisition 44 epigraph (the charitable choir on the Cloister road; the 416 taking is not mentioned). Stillwater lock dues and the board: Phase 16 text. The Bellwether as the drovers' house on the sheep-walk: Phase 22 text (landlord not named, since Gideon Thrale had it from his uncle). Dated 414: the Rift (413) is "last year"; the Bleach "the year before last" (412); Whisper-Grove still living; no Hedge yet. [PROPOSED] Jasper Fairweather, the Companion and its editions; the chain-yard foreman. Library: suits the Bonded Store at Stillwater if not the Bellwether. Owner ruling (Oct 2026): a volume stands. Vol I §§ Fortis, Skyships: every skyship has a Fortis-cut lodestone core that cancels mass; the manuscript's drift-glass lift-tanks give the lift.

title: The Overdue: Five Ghazals of the Dial Floor
author: Nadira al-Hassur; rendered into Low Common by a copying-clerk of the Tuners' Collegium
summary: Five linked poems by a widow of the Sandglass Bazaar who would not stop mourning when the contract said she must.
text: THE COPYIST'S NOTE

A ghazal is a chain of couplets, each ending on the same word or words, and in the last couplet the poet speaks to herself by name. Nadira al-Hassur's husband, Tahir, a caravan-factor, was lost on the Hourglass Erg in the Screaming Year. The term of mourning for a husband in the Bazaar is three hundred days. She kept them, and then she did not stop, and in 415 her House posted her as overdue. These five were passed from hand to hand on the Dial Floor. I have kept her refrains where Low Common would bear them, and let them limp where it would not.
I. FOR HOW LONG

They greet me on the Dial Floor and ask me, as they ask everyone: for how long?
The coffee-seller asks it, pouring. The dome hisses it all day: for how long?
Three hundred days is the term for a husband. I kept them to the hour.
On the three hundred and first I woke, and the pillow said: for how long?
The sand outside the glass was singing on the morning you rode out.
A tritone, my father would have said, and turned the camels round. It did not ask for how long.
All my life I have answered every question with a number.
Ask me again, neighbour. Watch my mouth, and see what it does with: for how long?
Nadira, they have written you overdue. Let them. Let the term run out.
In the sealed rooms under the Bazaar the clocks run backward, and nobody asks them for how long.
II. ON SCHEDULE

My sister came to me with her grief on schedule and went home on schedule.
She wept the proper days, and on the proper morning dried her eyes on schedule.
The House sent a clerk with a paper, a kind man, a little bald,
to read me the clause. He was sorry. He was sorry on schedule.
In the Stasis Vaults your crate holds the hour they carried you in from the Erg.
There is sand in your beard. Nothing in that crate is kept to a schedule.
Each Nullday I go down the forty steps with a lamp.
The warden lets me in and says I am the only visitor he has who is not on schedule.
The hour-merchants on the Floor would buy a year of my life for a fair price.
I could sell them every year I have and still be weeping behind schedule.
Nadira, an overdue woman is a scandal, an open-ended thing, a foreigner.
Good. In the west, they say, the orchard people mourn with no term at all. I will learn their schedule.
III. STILL

They sealed you at the moment you were set down, and you are lying still.
In there it is always that one afternoon, and you are warm, and still.
I lay my palm on the glass of the lid. It is not cold. It is not anything.
The stasis-wright says not to. It upsets the seal. I keep it there still.
Your hand is on your chest where the caravan-master put it.
A grain of sand is falling from your sleeve. It has not landed. It is falling still.
They tell me that a crate opened after its term lets the hour go all at once:
every hour you missed, arriving together. I would rather have you still.
Nadira, you have laid a man down like dial-wine, fifty years in an afternoon.
They say the wine tastes hollow. Everyone buys it. Everyone drinks it still.
IV. UNTIL THE TERM

On Dial Day every contract in the province ends at once, and everyone says: until the term.
The Floor is a riot of paper and the shouting of renewals. Until the term.
I went to the crate-house with the renewal in my hand and the fee in my purse.
I had signed it twice. Three years, and three years more. Until the term.
The clerk held out the pen. The pen waited. The whole dome seemed to wait,
the way the sand waits between one chord and the next. Until the term.
I gave him back the pen. I said: let it run. I said it to him and not to you.
He bowed, as they bow at doors when a guest goes out. Until the term.
Nadira, you who were never late for anything in your life,
you were late for this, and then on time. Go home. Until the term.
V. NONE

At the hour the lid came up, and the afternoon went out of the crate like a bird out of a sleeve.
Three years crossed your face in a breath. Then you were only a man at rest, and the term was none.
The grain of sand landed. I heard it. I am the only one who did.
We put you in the Erg at dusk, the old way, with the dunes holding a fifth. Their price was none.
My sister says: now. Now, surely, the mourning is done with the crate.
I tell her the crate had a term. I signed for it. The grief I never signed for has none.
Let the House post me. Let them write me into the book of the indecent.
I have read that book. It is full of the names of people who loved past the date, and its index is none.
Nadira, they call you open-ended, overdue, a foreigner in your own Bazaar.
Write it on the contract, then. Under how long, write: none.
notes: Canon: Vol I III.5 and Vol II Realm V (Sandglass Bazaar under the acoustic dome that breaks the sand's voice into a white hiss; "For how long?" and "Until the term"; grief "on schedule" or "overdue"; "open-ended" as an insult meaning sentimental and foreign; scheduled mourning; stasis crates that hold bodies and a moment; the Stasis Vaults and sealed rooms where clocks run backwards; dial-wine, aged fifty years in an afternoon, said to taste hollow; Dial Day, when every term in the province expires at once; dunes that chord, storms that scream in a key; Caravan-Master Oric's turning back for a tritone is echoed but he is not named). Series Bible Part VI (hour-merchants who buy and sell hours of life; the Hourglass Erg). Vol VII §4 (Dial Day is the first Stasisday of Thawmonth). The Screaming Year (412). Vol I III.5 (Dunes funerals are not specified; burial in the Erg is invented). [PROPOSED] Nadira al-Hassur, Tahir, her House's posting of her as overdue in 415, the forty steps to the vaults and the Nullday visits, the three-year crate contracts, the "book of the indecent", burial in the dunes at dusk. Shelved in the Greenhall as a gift-book carried west by a cider-buyer from the Dunes; equally at home in the Bonded Store at Stillwater.

title: The Carrying of Ketil
author: anonymous; as it is said at Skarth in the Iron Peaks, written down by a carter
summary: A blunt mountain saga of a daughter who carries her dead father to the standing-ground while the weight of the world will not stay still.
text:
This is said standing.
Sit, and you are not listening.

Ketil of Skarth kept goats on the high shelf.
Grey goats. Bad-tempered. Good milk.
He had one daughter. Hild.
He had one son. Arnulf.
The son was light.
That is all that needs saying of the son.

In the tide-month the mountain forgets its sums.
A stone weighs a stone at breakfast.
At noon it weighs a cart.
At dusk a goat floats off the shelf, bleating,
and comes down a mile off, surprised.
The Peaks were not always like this.
The old men say so. The old men are heavy.
We believe them.

Ketil died in the tide-month.
He sat down on the shelf with the milk-pail.
He did not get up.
That is how a heavy man dies. Sitting. Nothing spilt.

The dead of Skarth are not laid down.
Laid down, a man is only a man.
Stood up, the mountain carries him.
The standing-ground is above the shelf, under the Tooth.
Half a day's climb with a goat.
With a father, longer.

Arnulf said: wait for the tide to turn.
Hild said: the tide does not wait.
Arnulf said: the priest will come in the thaw.
Hild said: the priest is light.
She took the rope.

She put her father on her back
and tied him to her
the way you tie a kid that cannot walk.
His beard was in her ear.
He smelled of goat. He always had.

At the first cairn he weighed what a father weighs.
At the second cairn he weighed what a house weighs.
Her knees went into the scree.
She did not set him down.
Set down, a man that heavy stays down.
She stood in the scree until her legs were stone.
Then the tide went over,
and he weighed what a father weighs again,
and she went on.

At the third cairn he weighed nothing.
This was worse.
He rose off her back like a held breath.
The rope sang.
He wanted the sky. The sky wanted him.
She lay on the rock and held the rope
and the dead man stood up on the air above her
with his arms out
like a man about to dance at a wedding,
which he never did, being heavy.
She held.
She told him: not yet.
She told him: you are not light.
I will not have it said.

Night. Cold. The Tooth black on the stars.
The tide turned at the dead hour.
He came down into her arms
and weighed what a father weighs.

At the standing-ground the stone was soft.
Under the Tooth, where the old dead stand,
the ground gave under her heel
like bread.
She heard no ring when she struck it.
Only the dull thing. The dead note.
A light woman runs from that.
Hild did not run.
Running is heavy. Heavy goes through.
She stepped back in her own footprints,
one, and one, and one,
and she dug where the rock still rang,
and she stood him up in it,
and she put the stones about his knees,
and the mountain took his weight.

That was the bargain.
She had carried him far enough.
The mountain would carry him the rest.

She came down at noon.
Arnulf was at the shelf, milking.
He did not ask. She did not tell.
The goats were bad-tempered. Good milk.

At the fair in the thaw a stranger asked her,
the way it is asked:
You're heavy?
She said: heavy enough.
She did not say what she was carrying.
She was carrying him still.

This is said standing.
Now you may sit.
notes: Canon: Series Bible Part VI, the Iron Peaks (gravity-tides make weight wander; a sentry floats off the wall-walk; peak-folk bury their dead standing so the mountain can carry them) and Part IV (Mass law-rot: gravity-tides, "a child who suddenly weighs a ton"). Vol II Realm IV and Vol V §1 (dialect "You're heavy?" / "Heavy enough"; "light" as the worst word for a person; the dead note when tapped stone does not ring; "running is heavy, and heavy goes through"; step back in your own footprints). Vol II Appendix C (blunt Norse-Germanic, one syllable preferred). Dated c. 409, after the bleeding of the Anchors began (Siphon Wars from 398), so the old men can remember the mountain before the tides. [PROPOSED] Ketil, Hild and Arnulf of Skarth; Skarth itself; the Tooth and the standing-ground under it; the tide-month; the convention that the saga is said standing. Shelved at the Oakhaven watchhouse as a soldier's book; it would sit equally well in the Conservatory library.

title: Songs of the Long Mole: Shanties of the Rust Coast, with Their Soundings
author: collected by Jacomina Roe, printer, of Broadsheet Row
summary: Five working songs of Port Cantabile, taken down from pilots, widows and wet-nurses by a printer who explains what each one is for.
text: TO WHOEVER BUYS THIS

A Coast shanty is not for pleasure. It is a chart you can carry in your mouth. The verses hold the pitch of the reefs, the set of the current and the turn of the channel, and a captain who forgets a verse loses a ship. That was so when I was a girl, and it is still so, with two differences.

The first is that we sing them low now. In the Screaming Year a capstan chorus on the Long Mole brought the first hounds in off the harbour, and since then every song on this Coast has been sung under the breath, the way you would sing to a sleeping child in a house with thin walls. The second is that the coral has gone flat since the Fracture, by a hair, so the old soundings are a hair wrong, and the pilots sing them flat on purpose to come out right. I have printed the words as they were. Sing them a little low, in both senses.
I. WHAT'S SHE SINGING
The greeting of the harbour, made into a pilot's catechism. One voice asks; the leadsman answers; the helmsman steers by the answer.

What's she singing? She's singing high.
Then the Cay's awash and the Grinners are dry.
Keep the Mole-light over your starboard rail,
and the Grinners will grin, but they'll not get your sail.

What's she singing? She's singing low.
Then the bar's gone soft where it used to show.
Lay her off by a cable, lay her off by two,
for the sand that held your father won't hold you.

What's she singing? She's singing wrong.
Then she's changed her key and the channel's gone.
Hand the lead, hand the lead, and the lead again,
and say what she's singing to the next poor men.
The last verse is new since the Fracture. My father never sang it. Every pilot I asked has sung it to me, and not one of them would say who made it.
II. CHORUS TO YOU

On the Coast a debt is holy, and the oath is "I'm chorus to you": I owe you, and I will pay, if not in coin then in the singing of your verse when you cannot. This one is sung at the capstan when a ship is warped out owing money, which is most of them.

I'm chorus to you for the rope and the tar,
I'm chorus to you for the drink at the bar,
I'm chorus to you for the berth and the bread,
and I'll sing out your verse if they number you dead.

So heave, and she'll go, and heave, and she's free,
and the sea takes the rest, and the rest is the sea.
The Harbour-Queen is said to dislike this song. It is said she dislikes it because it is true.
III. THE MOLE-BELL

When a soul goes into the water, the bell at the Mole-head is struck once. Once for each. It is not rung for traitors. This is sung by the women on the Mole while they wait for a boat that is late, and it is the only song on the Coast that has no soundings in it at all, because it is not meant to bring anybody in.

One for the man who went over the side,
one for the boy that the tide took wide,
one for the wife at the top of the Stair
who counts them, and counts them, and counts them there.

Strike it once, and once is enough.
The sea does the rest of the ringing.
IV. THE BOTTLE

Since the Screaming Year there has been a trade on this Coast in bottles held over the trench with the stopper out, to catch what comes up. Some say it is the voices of the drowned. I will not argue with a widow about what she has heard in her own kitchen. But here is the song the old hands teach the young ones, and every line of it was paid for by somebody.

Not in the harbour and not in the hold,
not on a deck, however you're told,
not by a lantern, not for a lark,
open her out at sea, and dark.

And if it goes quiet, you know what to do:
the maul to the seacock, and over with you,
and row for the light that the Mole-bell shows,
and never look back at the place where it goes.

A note for landsmen. A quiet goes to the light. That is why no Coast man takes a lantern into a hold that has gone silent, and why the song tells you to open a bottle in the dark. I do not know more than that, and I have not tried to.
V. WENDMERE RINGS THREE

This is the newest song in the book and the one I sing myself. Wendmere was a fishing town south of the Cay. The trench opened under it in '13 and it went down whole, tower and all, and since that first winter its bell has rung under the water, out past the Cay, three strokes and a silence, three strokes and a silence, every night of the year. Nobody has rowed out to see what rings it. The opinion of the Coast is that a bell which rings the drowned to sleep is doing a service, and that you do not go poking at a service. The Lantern Yard learned to sleep by it within the month. The wet-nurses made this to its count, and there is hardly a child in the lower town who has gone to sleep without it.

Hush now, hush, and listen to me,
out past the Cay, Wendmere rings three.
One for the boats and one for the bay,
and one for the people who went away.

Hush now, hush, and what does it say?
It says they're sleeping under the bay.
It says the water is kind and deep,
and it rings for them so that they can sleep.

Three for the drowned and three for the deep,
and three for my darling, and go to sleep.
notes: Canon: Vol II Realm VI and Vol IV Book Three (shanties encode navigation and a captain who forgets one loses a ship; "What's she singing?"; "I'm chorus to you" as the debt oath; the reefs change key with the tide; the Long Mole and the Mole-bell; the Cay; the Lantern Yard, where the first vox-bottle was opened; Wendmere, drowned by the trench, whose Chime "rang in threes for six years" and the whole harbour learned to sleep by it). Vol V §2 (one stroke of the Mole-bell for each soul in the water, not rung for traitors). Series Bible Part VI and Book Two notes (the singing coral's note has wandered flat since the Fracture; the Harbour-Queen; quiets come aboard through vox-bottles and go to the light, so the Harbour will not take lanterns into a hold). Vol IV §1.5 (listening through a reed, breath coming back off the wax, the maul to the seacock if the reed goes dead), here given as common Coast lore in a song, not as Vesper's protocol. Manuscript Ch4 (the first hounds came in off the harbour in the Screaming Year). The collector does not know what rings the Chime and says nobody has looked; the truth (Vol IV) is not revealed. Dated 417, while the Chime still rings. [PROPOSED] Jacomina Roe; the Grinners (a reef); the songs and their verses; the claim that the capstan chorus on the Mole drew the first hounds; Wendmere drowning in '13 (Vol IV says only that the trench drowned it and the bell rang six years). Shelved below decks on the Kestrel as a Rust Coast crew's songbook.

title: Keep Talking: Letters from the Wall
author: Wystan Hobday, penal legionnaire One-Forty-Seven of Null-Watch, to his sister Meggy of Greenroot Hamlet
summary: A Greenroot man sent to the penal legion at Null-Watch writes home to a sister who cannot read, and does not stop talking.
text: These were kept in the chapel at Greenroot, folded in the back of the parish book, because Meggy Hobday could not read and they were read to her there, by whoever had the reading that week.

I.
To be read to Meggy Hobday at the chapel at Greenroot, if somebody would be so kind.
Null-Watch. Lambmonth, I am told, of '15. The third hour of the night. They count from the dark here, Meggy, not from the clock.

Here I am then. I am well. They have given me a coat with lead sewn in the hem so I walk like Granda did after the cider, and a number, which is One-Forty-Seven. I may not sign my name. Nobody signs his name. They say names draw the Quiet, and you get yours back when you are discharged. So if this comes signed with a number it is still your brother, the one who took the Reeve's mutton in the hungry winter and would do it again, and you can tell the Reeve so, quietly.

The first rule here is you keep talking. That is the whole of the law, near enough. You talk all day, and in your sleep if you can manage it. About anything. Onions. The days of the week. They give you a partner and you talk at him and he talks at you, and if he stops you shout for the sergeant before you look at him. Before. That is the order. My partner is a Peaks man, number Two-Thirty, who knows more about sheep than any man ought, and I know more about reeds, so we are well matched and we bore each other half to death, which is the idea.

II.
To be read to Meggy at the chapel.
Null-Watch. Firstfruit, '15. The second hour of the night.

Every morning at dawn the whole wall fires. Forty batteries along four miles of black stone, all at once, out over the edge. It is not shot. It is noise. It is the biggest no in the world, Meggy, said every morning, and they call it the Refusal, and I have stood at a gun for it sixty mornings now and my ears ring like the oaks at home.

The General does not speak. She lost her voice on this wall the first night of the Rift. She talks with her knuckles on her breastplate, and there is a man who speaks for her, and when she strikes four flat blows it means the Watch holds the wall and everybody straightens up without knowing why.

There are monks here in lead hoods who stand along the edge and never say a word. And there is one word you must not say. It is the word for what you get in a church when the reed stops. A man said it at supper and the man beside him knocked him off the bench, and the sergeant saw it and ate his soup. That is how serious they are.
Does the little one's reed still sound over your door? Tell me it does.

III.
To be read to Meggy at the chapel.
Null-Watch. Ashfall, '15. I do not know the hour. Late.
I have been trying to write this for a week and I will just say it.

On the lip-walk, at the first hour, Two-Thirty stopped. In the middle of a ewe. He had her halfway through lambing and he stopped. I looked at him, which I should not have done first, and his face was surprised, and then it was not surprised, and then it was the face you have when you put down a heavy load at the end of the day. And he turned and went toward the edge, not fast. Like a man walking home.

I got him by the collar and I talked. I do not know what I said. I think I told him the whole of the Greenroot reed-beds, bed by bed, and who cut which, and he came back in at the end of it like a man coming out of the river, and he was angry with me. He was angry, Meggy, as if I had woken him.
There was no sound. I keep wanting to say what it sounded like. That is the thing. Nothing did.
He went to listen in Frostmonth, on a night I was in the infirmary with my hand. That is what they say here. Gone to listen. Never deserted. I have a new partner now.

IV.
To be read to Meggy at the chapel.
Null-Watch. Seedmonth, '16. The fourth hour.
Some new men up from the west this spring, one of them a Fenwick man, in for debt, who can talk about the price of lamp-oil for an hour together without drawing breath. We call him the Almanac.

We had a Discharge on Driftday. I will tell you how they do it, because you would want to know. They do not bury here and they do not weep out loud. The General lays her hand flat on the man's chest and taps on it, with one finger, his name and his place and his service, and then Discharged, and her voice says it all after her. And then the whole Watch stops talking. All of us. For three breaths. On this wall that is the most dangerous thing a man can do, and we do it on purpose, for him. And then somebody says Rootday, and his voice cracks on it, and we all say Hearthday, Massday, and on round the week, and go on.
That is how you get your name back here. I mean to get mine back the other way, at the gate, with a coat on.

V.
To be read to Meggy at the chapel.
Null-Watch. Lambmonth, '17. The third hour.

Two years. I am learning the General's cant. I can tell holds from goes, and I can tell the blow that means well done, which she has struck once at me, on the gun at the Refusal, when the breech stuck and I cleared it.

The old women at home used to say do your weeping on paper, and there is a book here from the garrison press that says it too. I have done mine. You have had all of it, I think, and so has the clerk at the Organum who reads these on the way through, and hello to him.

This is all talk, Meggy. That is the trick of the place. I will write again at Reedmonth. Kiss the little one. Hum to her. Not too loud, and not too quiet.
One-Forty-Seven, that was and is your brother.

VI.
In another hand, larger, slower.
To the sister of One-Forty-Seven, at Greenroot in the Reach, to be read to her.
Null-Watch. Reedmonth, '17.
He asked me to write if. So I am writing.
The breech of the second gun on Battery Eleven let go at the Refusal four days back. He was on it. It was quick. He was talking. He was telling the boy beside him how you cut a reed so it sounds.

The General laid her hand on him and tapped it out, and her voice said it after her, and that was the first time I ever heard his name, though I had stood next to him two years. We were quiet for him three breaths. Then I said Rootday, because I was nearest.
I am to tell you he was not afraid of the edge. That was true. I am to tell you he was well fed. That was nearly true.
He could never put it at the bottom of these. So I am putting it here, for him, where it belongs.
Wystan Hobday, of Greenroot. Discharged.
Fifty-Two
notes: Canon: Series Bible Part VI (Null-Watch, obsidian and lead, dampening cannons firing white noise; every legionnaire wears lead) and Part VII (the penal legion; Theresa Ward, mute since 413, commanding in iron-cant; the Lead Brothers). Vol VI §1 (forty batteries on four miles; Standing Order Nine, keep talking; the face going startled, then not, then peaceful, walking toward the edge "like a man walking home"; iron-cant, four flat blows for "the Watch holds the wall"; the General's "voice"; the Discharge: hand flat on the chest, tapping name, place, service and Discharged, three breaths of silence, then someone says Rootday; the Lead Brothers do not intervene). Vol II Realm VIII (rota numbers in service because names invite the Quiet, names returned at discharge; "gone to listen", never deserted; "Quiet" as the one true profanity, striking a man who says it not punished; alarm before checking). Vol VII §5 (the Watch counts hours from the dark). Manuscript epigraph, A Plain Account of the Cacophony, Null-Watch Press ("do your weeping on paper"). Vol VI §1 (Elric Orrel, 94, of Fenwick, penal legion from 416 for debt, who talked about the price of lamp-oil): he appears only as "a Fenwick man" with those canon facts; his nickname is [PROPOSED]. The Cascade famine (Series Bible, Aldric Vance). The Shelf and the baskets are deliberately not mentioned. [PROPOSED] Wystan and Meggy Hobday and her child; Two-Thirty and Fifty-Two; the theft of the Reeve's mutton; letters routed through the Organum and read there; the breech failure on Battery Eleven in Reedmonth 417; the letters kept in the Greenroot parish book.

title: On the Constancy of the Light: A Treatise for the Provinces
author: Canon Placidus Sorell of the Basilica, Sol-Luminary; rendered into Low Common by Eustace Garner, curate
summary: A Canon of Sol-Luminary explains to the lesser provinces, kindly and at length, why the Light is the first of the laws and can never fail.
text: THE TRANSLATOR TO THE READER

This little work was written for the instruction of the faithful in the provinces below the cloud, and it is my privilege to put it into the common tongue for the chapels of the Reach. I have rendered the Canon's remarks upon our own province faithfully, as a translator must, and I ask the reader to receive them in the spirit of a physician's candour, which can sting and is meant to heal. E. G., at the Chapel of the Pure Note, Oakhaven.
I. OF THE ORDER OF THE LAWS
Every child is taught that the world is held up by eight Spires, and that each Spire sings one law. It is less often taught, and it is time it was, that the eight are not equal.

Consider them. Growth is a rustic law. It knows one word, which is more, and says it to the cabbage and the cancer alike. Heat is a law of furnaces and its people are scarred and loud. Mass is a law of weight, which is to say of falling. Time is a merchant's law and keeps accounts. Velocity is the law of sailors and of the late misfortune in the Valley, which I attribute, in charity, to the coarseness of that law and not to any fault of its stewards. Memory is a melancholy law. Decay is not spoken of at table.

And Light? Light is the law by which all the others are seen. Without it Growth would be a rumour in the dark, and Heat would be a cough in a cellar, and Mass would be a thing that bumps you. It is the first law, because it is the condition of the others being known at all, and its note, five hundred and twenty-eight, is the note to which every Sovereign rings when it is dropped upon a good floor. The coin of the realm agrees with me. I can think of no higher authority below the Basilica.
II. OF THE ONE NOTE
Q. What is holiness? A. One note, held without end. Q. What is sin? A. The second note.

The provincial reader will forgive me if I press this upon him, for he lives where it is least observed. I have heard the Cantors of the orchard country, on a visit made in my youth, sing two notes together over a sick child, and I do not doubt their kindness, but kindness is not the measure of a thing. The second note is a crack in the bell. A people who sing in two notes will in time think in two minds, and a man of two minds will cast a shadow, as we say here, at noon.
The Light sings one note and has sung it since the world was pinned. It does not harmonise. It does not need to. It is entire.
III. OF SHADOW

A shadow is the place where the Light has been refused. It is not wicked in itself, any more than a stain is wicked; but it is a refusal, and a refusal repeated becomes a habit, and a habit becomes a province. I say nothing against the orchard country, whose cider I have taken with gratitude. I say only that it is green and dim at noon, and that a people who live under leaves must take especial care of their souls.

In Sol-Luminary we build so that no wall throws a shadow on another. Our children do not know the word for the dark side of a street. When they go down below the cloud they are sick for a week, and I count that sickness an honour to them.
IV. OF THE GLASS

The Aether-Glass that comes from the Dawning Spire is the Light's surplus, as all the Synod's learned agree: a generosity so great that it overflows the stone. It is blue at the root, as a flame is blue at the root, and pale as it cools. There are those who say the drawing of it wearies the Spire. These are people who have never stood beneath the Spire. It does not weary. You may as well say the sun is tired of rising.
V. OF THE DAWN

Every morning of the world the Sky Choirs have sung the dawn service, and every morning the dawn has come, and the faithless say this is a coincidence. I say it is an answer. The Light is attended. It is sung to, in its own note, as a king is addressed in his own tongue, and it is pleased.

It is spoken of in the Basilica that a greater offering is being prepared, a unison such as has not been sung in the history of the Church. I may not say more. I will say that I have stood beneath the Spire at sunrise, when the chord comes down the mountain over two hours like a tide of gold, and that I have never heard so much as a tremor in it, and that I do not expect to in my lifetime, or in yours, or in the lifetime of the world.
VI. A CONSOLATION FOR THE PROVINCES

Let the lesser provinces take comfort. Your oaks may ring and your sands may sing. Your weights may wander and your seas may forget themselves. Here and there a law may falter; we hear of a valley where the rain stands still. But look up. Whatever else in the world may fail, the Light will not fail. The red of the Sol-Luminary rose is the reddest thing in creation, and it will be as red when your grandchildren's grandchildren come up the chains to see it.
Of all things under heaven, this alone is certain: the Light does not tire.
notes: Canon: Series Bible Part III "What everyone believes" (the Architects pinned the world to eight Spires, each singing one law; Aether-Glass is the Light's generous surplus; the catechism Q and A, also the manuscript's opening epigraph); Part VI (Dawning Heights; the Spire; 528 Hz) and Part IV (everyone over thirty remembers when red was redder: the treatise's rose is dramatic irony). Prologue (glass from the Spire is blue like the bottom of a flame; the Church's teaching that the Spire sings one note; the Light "relieved of its excess"). Vol I III.2 and Vol II Realm II (dawn audible as a rising chord over two hours; architecture built to eliminate shadow; shadows indecent; lowlanders sickened; "casts" meaning vulgar; dawn service compulsory). Vol I §4.4 (the Sovereign rings at 528 when dropped). Vol III Appendix (the Basilica). The Valley of Velocity broke in 398 (Vol III (b)). Written 410, before the Rite (411–412), so the "greater offering" is only rumoured; nothing of the Rite's purpose is stated. The High Patriarch is not named. [PROPOSED] Canon Placidus Sorell; Eustace Garner, curate of the Chapel of the Pure Note at Oakhaven, as translator; the Sol-Luminary rose. Its readers are the Chapel's; a copy could also sit in the Conservatory library, where Cantors would keep it for the paragraph about them.

title: A Lantern on the Basin: A Widow's Journey to Whisper-Grove
author: Tabitha Fernly, of Greenroot Hamlet in the Reach
origin: printed at Oakhaven for the author
summary: A Reach widow walks to Whisper-Grove to say her son's name aloud on the night of the lanterns, and writes down the city that took her in.
text: I am not a writer and this is not a proper book. The printer at Oakhaven says it will make forty copies and that is a book whether I like it or not. I am writing it for anyone in the Reach who has a name they cannot say, and for the Lantry house in the Bell Yard, who will laugh at it.

My son Rafe went out to the reed-beds at Greenroot in the Screaming Year to bring in the last of the cutting, and he did not come home, and there was nothing to bring home. It was the hounds, we think. In the Reach we bury our dead in silence, and the Cantor sings them down, and that is right, and I would not change it. But I had nothing to bury and nothing for the Cantor to sing over, and so for three years Rafe was not buried and not anything. I could not say his name. If I said it in the house it went nowhere. If I said it outside I was afraid of what might hear, and answer.

The carter's wife at Greenroot, who is from the Woods by her mother, told me that in Whisper-Grove there is a night every year when the water in the plazas is highest, and the people float paper lanterns on the long basin, one for each of their dead, and say each name aloud as they set it down. And she said that there, a name said aloud is never lost, because the whole Grove remembers it for you.
So I went.
THE ROAD

From Greenroot the road goes east through the orchards and then the orchards stop being ours. You will know the Woods by the willows. They are silver, not green, and they weep right down into pools that shine from underneath, so that at dusk your own face is lit from the chin like a child telling a ghost story. The mist is the colour of lilac, and it lies at the height of your knees all day, and you walk through it like a woman wading. There are no birds. I noticed that on the second day and it frightened me, and the carter I rode with said, kindly, that there never were, and that the Woods did not miss them.

I had expected the people of the Woods to be sad, because the Woods look sad. They are not. They are the most courteous people I have ever met. The carter called me "little mother" from the first mile, though I am older than him, and every woman at every well called me "dear one", and at the inn on the third night the landlord's girl asked if I would like my supper "now, or presently, or when you are quite ready, dearling", and I cried, which was foolish, and she did not seem to think so.
THE CITY

Whisper-Grove is marble, white marble gone soft and grey with moss, and it is sunk into its own hollow so that you come down to it by steps from every side, and the great spire of the Canopy stands over all of it, wood and crystal grown together, so high that the top of it is in the mist and you cannot tell where it stops.

I lodged with the Lantry house in the Bell Yard, which the carter's wife had written to. There are nine of them, three of them children, and old Isbet Lantry at the head of the table, who is eighty and has a voice like warm milk. They gave me the room at the top of the stair, which is very steep, and Nonie, who is six, showed me the pools in the courtyard. She said the pools remember. I looked into one and saw a kitchen I have never stood in, and a woman's floury hands, and a loaf going into an oven, and it was not frightening at all. Nonie said that is only somebody's morning, and somebody always lets you have a bit of theirs.

In the evenings, from the Cloister road, you can hear the children of the charitable choir at their practice behind shut doors. They sing very low, in the Narrow, as we do at home. I did not know that children could sing so quietly and so clear. Old Isbet said they are the pride of the Grove and the despair of their teachers, both.
THE NIGHT OF THE LANTERNS

The Weeping Plaza is a square of white marble the size of four fields, with a colonnade on three sides and the Moot-house on the fourth, and down the middle of it runs a long shallow basin. On the night the water is highest, it is brimming, and lit from under, and still.

They came down in the dusk from every street. Thousands. Old Isbet said seventy thousand live in the Grove and every one of them comes, and I believe it, because I have never seen so many people and heard so little. They do not crowd. They wait their turn at the edge of the water. Each one kneels, and sets a paper lantern on the basin, and says a name aloud, not loud, but aloud; and then, this is the thing, the people nearest say the name after them. Softly. So that it is said by more than one mouth, and held by more than one.

I had made my lantern at the Lantry table, badly, and Nonie had mended it. When it came to me I knelt down at the water with my knees wet through and I could not do it. Three years. My mouth would not.
Old Isbet put her hand on my back, and waited, as if we had all night. Then I said it.
"Rafe Fernly."

And the Lantry house said it after me, all nine of them, and the strangers beside them said it, and the strangers beside those, a little way along the basin, so that I heard my son's name go away from me along the water in other people's voices, kindly, the way you pass a child along a line of hands to keep him out of a river.
The lantern went out on the basin with all the others. There were so many that the whole plaza was lit, and the mist over it, and the colonnade threw its shadows up into the fog.
COMING HOME
I am home at Greenroot now. I have said his name four times since, in my own kitchen, and nothing has answered, and nothing has heard, and that is right.

I will go back to the Grove next year for the lanterns, and I will take this book with me. I will give one copy to the Lantry house, who will laugh at how I have made them sound grander than they are, and say their stair is not so steep. And I will leave one at the Moot-house, on the shelf where they keep the books that travellers bring, so that the next woman from the Reach who has a name she cannot say will know where to lodge, and what to do, and that she will be welcome.
In Whisper-Grove nothing is ever forgotten. I have left him there, where he is safe.
notes: Canon: Manuscript Ch14 (the Weeping Plaza, white marble the size of four fields, colonnade on three sides and the Moot-house on the fourth, a shallow ornamental basin where the city floated lamps on festival nights before the water table rose in 416; the Bell Yard; shadows thrown up onto the fog). Vol VII (b) §4 (the Drowned Lanterns: one lantern per name, read aloud by whoever sets it, on the night the Grove's water is highest; the pre-416 form on the basin is implied by Ch14). Vol II Realm VII (pre-silencing Grove speech formal, warm, full of diminutives; no birds; lilac mist; faces lit from the chin by the pools; the Canopy spire of fused wood and crystal). Series Bible Part VI (silver willows, phosphorescent pools, reflecting pools showing strangers' memories; 74,000 people). Manuscript Requisition 44 epigraph and Ch17 (the charitable choir on the Cloister road), and Book One's Reach burial custom (bound jaw, stone on the tongue, which Book Four Part One dates from 417, so not used in this 415 book). The Narrow and "never answer a voice you cannot see" (Series Bible Part IV). Dated 415, the year before the Silencing; nothing of 416 is foreseen. [PROPOSED] Tabitha and Rafe Fernly; the Lantry household of the Bell Yard (Isbet, Nonie); the carter's wife; the forty copies; the Moot-house shelf of travellers' books (this suits the planned Moot-house library). The last line is irony only for a reader who finds the book in the silenced city.

title: Instructions to Persons Visiting the Bastion
author: Keld Holm, Clerk of Visitors, for the Martial Compact of Fortis
summary: The rules every carter, factor and pilgrim is handed at the gate of Fortis, written by a clerk who means every word and wastes none.
text: Issued at the Lower Gate to every person not of the Compact. Read it before the second terrace. There is no third copy.
1. You will be asked: "You're heavy?" Answer: "Heavy enough." Do not answer "Yes". Do not answer "Very". Do not tell the sentry what you ate. He is asking whether you are yourself. Say that you are.
2. Do not offer your hand to anyone. In the Bastion a hand offered to a stranger is a claim on his weight. If a man of the Compact offers you his, he has decided something about you. Take it.
3. Do not call any person light. Not in jest. Not of a child. Not of yourself, in the tavern, at the end of a long day. It is the worst thing that can be said here, and it is not said.

4. Weight wanders in the Peaks. Your pack may weigh twice on the fourth terrace what it weighed at the gate, and nothing at all by noon. Hold it by the strap, not the buckle. If it rises, let it go up a little and bring it down slowly. Do not chase it. The Compact does not refund carriage, and does not pay for goods that have floated.
5. Iron goes sideways in the mist. On the outer stair, carry your knife inside your coat. A dropped knife does not go down here. It goes over.

6. Do not run on any terrace. Running is heavy, and heavy goes through. If the ground before you feels soft, or wrong, or like bread, stop. Step backward, slowly, in your own footprints, or in the footprints of the person ahead. Then tell a sentry. He will thank you. He will not thank you twice.

7. You will hear tapping in the lower levels: the Sounders, testing the floor with their rods. This is a good sound. If the tapping stops, turn round and go back the way you came. Do not ask why. Do not wait to see. They will tell you if they want you to know, and they will not want you to know.

8. The Weighing Hall, on the third terrace, is open to visitors on every day but the Weighing itself, which falls on the first Massday of Sheafmonth. Uncover your head. When a soldier of the Compact dies his kit is weighed, and the weight is cut in the wall beside his name. Do not touch the wall. There is no room left at the height of a hand. The new names are cut higher now, and the masons use a ladder.

9. The dead of the Peaks are buried standing, so that the mountain can carry them. You may see this done. Do not remark on it. Do not ask whether it is uncomfortable for them. A visitor asked that in the spring. He was not answered, and he left by the next cart.

10. Prices are fixed and are not discussed. Every scale in the Bastion is checked against the Marshal's weight, so the weight you are charged is the true weight, whatever your pack did on the stair. Sovereigns are taken. Chimes are not. Promises are not.
11. Visitors may not go on the Wall. If you find yourself on the Wall, you are no longer a visitor, and these instructions no longer apply to you. Others will.

12. If the bell on the Wall is struck in threes, go indoors, to the nearest door that opens, and stay there. Any door in the Bastion will open to a stranger when that bell is struck. That is the oldest law in Fortis, and it has never once been broken.

13. If a member of your party is lost within the Bastion, go to the Clerk of Visitors. The Compact will weigh what he carried, if anything is left, and cut the weight in the wall of the Weighing Hall with his name and the year, in the visitors' row by the west door. He does not have to be of the Compact. He has only to have been heavy. We have done it for carters. We have done it for a pedlar's boy. It costs you nothing. Do not offer to pay.
14. Persons who say that these instructions are short are reminded that they are the weight they need to be.
15. On leaving. Your pack will be lighter on the road down. This is the mountain, and not your purse. Count your purse anyway.

Heavy enough.
K. Holm, Clerk of Visitors.
notes: Canon: Vol V §1 (the Culture of Weight: "You're heavy?" / "Heavy enough"; light as the worst thing said of a person; do not offer your hand to a stranger, a claim on their weight; the Marshal's tuning-weight against which every scale is checked; "Running is heavy, and heavy goes through"; step backward in the footsteps of the person ahead; the Sounders with tuned rods, and the dead note; the Weighing Hall on the third terrace, kit weighed and the weight cut beside the name, tens of thousands of names). Vol VII §4 (the Weighing, Keystone, on the first Massday of Sheafmonth, 7 Sheafmonth by the formula). Series Bible Part VI (gravity-tides, the shield that weighs eighty pounds, peak-folk bury their dead standing). Vol II Realm IV hazards (magnetic mist pulls metal sideways; dropped weapons go over the edge, not down) and Vol I §4.4 (Chimes still accepted in the Archipelago and the Dunes, so plausibly refused here). The Compact-Marshal is not named for 416. [PROPOSED] Keld Holm and the office of Clerk of Visitors; the Lower Gate; the bell struck in threes and the law that any door opens to a stranger; the visitors' row in the Weighing Hall; masons cutting names on ladders; the visitor who asked about standing burial. Shelved at the quarry's Depot Three, where Consortium engineers bound for the arsenal would carry it; it also suits the Bonded Store at Stillwater, beside the timber ledger.

title: Ledger and Day-Book of a Timber Run, Stillwater to Fortis
author: Rowland Ruddock, timber factor, of Stillwater Landing
origin: Stillwater Landing, and the road east
summary: A Stillwater timber factor keeps his accounts on a run of ringing iron-bough to the Bastion, and finds one entry he cannot price.
text:
Hearthday, 2 Seedmonth, at Stillwater.
Bought of the Timber Compact cutters, forty logs of iron-bough, felled at the first frost, seasoned, chalked for Fortis. Paid: 20 sovereigns.
Paid the keeper his lock dues, in advance, not refunded. Paid: 1 sovereign.
Paid the keeper for news of the river. Paid: 1 sovereign. He sold the same to the Compact's man before me and the Bores factor after, and told me so, which I suppose is what I paid for.
Hired Huw and Dickon to raft, and Bartle to pole. Wages advanced, 2 sovereigns each. Paid: 6 sovereigns.
Took my nephew Seb, fifteen, because his mother asked me, and because she asked me loudly.

Stasisday, 4 Seedmonth.
Out through the lower lock at first light. The basin carries; we said nothing until the cutting. Every lashing oiled so it will not creak. Every log wrapped at the ends in old fleece, so that if two touch they knock and do not ring. Paid for fleece: 4 pence. The rule on the raft is the rule of the trade: no log touches another, and no man raises his voice, and nobody whistles, and that includes you, Seb.

Driftday, 6 Seedmonth.
At the Drop the raft took the weir crooked and the big log at the head, the best of the forty, came out of its fleece and struck the sill. It rang. I have heard iron-bough ring all my life and I have never heard it ring like that, over water, at dusk, like the Chapel bell at the Landing.
There were hounds on the east bank inside the count of twenty. Huw did not wait for me to tell him. He cut the head log loose with the hatchet and kicked it off down the race, and it went away down the river ringing every time it touched a stone, and the hounds went with it along the bank, and we lay flat on the raft and let the current have us the other way.
Item: one log, the best, given to the river. Value 3 sovereigns. Entered here for the record, but not added, since I paid for it already at Stillwater and do not mean to pay for it twice. It bought something. I am not sure the ledger has a column for what.

Rootday, 9 Seedmonth, the railhead at Ironford.
Thirty-nine logs onto the flatcars of the Iron Tramway. Freight: 8 sovereigns. The yard clerk would not take Chimes, though I had them. Paid him besides, for his consideration, which is what he called it: 1 sovereign.

Dawnday, 13 Seedmonth.
The Tramway goes round the Valley of Velocity by the long loop, and from the cars you can see down into it. It is raining in the Valley. It has been raining in the Valley, the brakeman says, since '98, the same rain, hanging in the air like beads on threads, and the light goes through it and does not come out the same colour. Nobody runs on the cars. The brakeman told Seb so, and then told him again, and then showed him a man's boot nailed to the brake-house wall and did not say whose.
Seb bet Bartle a penny he could throw a stone into the Valley. He threw it. It went in at the edge and it is going still, I suppose, faster all the time. Bartle says the wager is not decided until it lands. Paid Seb's wager anyway, to have peace: 1 penny.

Rootday, 17 Seedmonth.
Into the Peaks. Grey rain, grey rock, and a mist that pulls at anything iron, so that Dickon's knife went out of his belt sideways and over the drop like a bird. At the second halt the axle under the fourth car began to groan, and the brakeman said the tide was on, and we watched the logs on that car sink the springs flat, as if each one weighed a house. Nobody touched them. In an hour the tide went over and the springs came back up and the logs were logs again.
A Peaks woman at the halt asked Huw "You're heavy?" and he said "Middling", and she looked at him the way you would look at a man who had spat on your doorstep. Seb has learned to say "Heavy enough" and says it to everybody, including the mules.
Food and lodging at the halts, the whole road. Paid: 2 sovereigns.

Driftday, 22 Seedmonth.
Seb asks about the Sounders, who walk ahead of the work-gangs on the line tapping the stone with iron rods as tall as themselves. He walked behind one for a mile this morning, at a respectful distance, listening. The Sounder let him.

Nullday, 24 Seedmonth.
No train runs on Nullday in the Peaks. We sat up in the halt-house all night with the hush-lamp and talked, the five of us, about nothing, so as not to be still. Seb asked what the dead note sounds like. Nobody knew. Dickon said if you have heard it you do not come back to say.

Massday, 27 Seedmonth, at Fortis.
Delivered thirty-nine logs to the Compact's quartermaster on the fourth terrace. They weighed them on Fortis scales, checked against the Marshal's own weight, and the logs weighed a fifth again what they weighed at Stillwater, and I said so, honestly, and the quartermaster said the weight is the weight, and paid by it, 2 sovereigns the log.
Received: 78 sovereigns.
I asked her what the Bastion wants with ringing wood, when it has the whole mountain. She said they use Reach iron-bough for props in the deep levels, because a prop of iron-bough rings when the load comes on it, and a Sounder can hear a ringing prop three levels off. Your wood tells us when the mountain moves, she said. It is the only timber in the world that will.
Paid Huw, Dickon and Bartle the balance of their wages, 3 sovereigns each: 9 sovereigns.

Rootday, 3 Lambmonth.
Seb has asked to stay. The Sounders take any boy who can stand still and listen, and the Captain of them tells me he can. I said his mother would have my hide. He said his mother would have it anyway, for the boots. I bought him boots fit for the deep. Paid: 2 sovereigns.
I have written to Joan. I have not posted it.

ACCOUNT OF THE RUN
Paid out: 50 sovereigns and 5 pence.
Received: 78 sovereigns.
Balance in hand: 28 sovereigns, less 5 pence.
Left at Fortis: one nephew, Sebastian Ruddock, fifteen, at his own asking.
I have looked for the column to put him in, and there is not one.
I go home lighter, which up here is an insult, and down there will only be the truth.
